title: Perform calf and heifer rearing, production and health care practices

lessons.title: Practical care from calving to weaning
lessons.html:
Your practical tasks

In this practical module you carry out and supervise the calf rearing routine. You must show that you can do each task correctly and keep the records that prove it.

At and after calving

  1. Prepare a clean, dry calving camp or pen and check close-up cows regularly.
  2. Recognise normal calving progress and call for help early when it is not progressing as the farm protocol describes; never pull a calf with excessive force or with a vehicle.
  3. After birth, clear the calf's airways and check breathing.
  4. Disinfect the navel as the protocol states.
  5. Tag and record the calf: number, dam, sex, date, birth difficulty.
  6. Feed colostrum promptly, in the volume set by the farm protocol, by bottle or by tube if trained and authorised.
  7. Record colostrum time, volume and quality reading if tested.

Daily milk feeding

  • Prepare milk or milk replacer to the exact concentration and temperature on the label or protocol; weigh powder, do not guess.
  • Feed at the same times every day.
  • Clean buckets, bottles and teats after every feed with hot water and detergent; let them dry.
  • Provide fresh water and calf starter from the first week; refresh starter daily.
  • Watch every calf drink. A calf that does not drink is the first sign of illness.

Daily health check

CheckProblem signs
AppetiteNot drinking milk, leaving starter
DungWatery, bloody or very smelly
BreathingCough, fast breathing, nasal discharge
AttitudeDull, ears drooping, sunken eyes
Navel and jointsSwollen, hot

Take temperatures of suspect calves, treat according to the vet's protocol (for example oral electrolytes for scours), isolate sick calves and record every case.

lessons.title: Weaning, heifer growth and health programmes
lessons.html:
Weaning

  • Wean calves when they eat the target amount of starter for several consecutive days, as the farm protocol sets.
  • Reduce milk gradually; avoid other stresses such as dehorning or moving groups at the same time.
  • Move weaned calves into small, even-sized groups.

Monitoring growth

Weigh calves and heifers with a scale or estimate with a weigh band at set ages. Record weights and compare with the farm's growth targets. Calves below target need investigation: feeding, disease, parasites or bullying.

Heifer management

  • Feed according to the ration for each age group; ensure adequate trough and water space.
  • Control internal and external parasites according to the vet's programme.
  • Monitor body condition; heifers should be well grown but not fat.
  • Record heats and inseminate at the target size and age set by the manager.
  • Confirm pregnancy at vet visits and move pregnant heifers to the correct group before calving.

Health programmes

  • Vaccinations: follow the farm's vet-designed schedule. Brucellosis vaccination of heifer calves is a legal requirement; the vet will set the age and approved vaccine.
  • Tick control: dip or pour-on as scheduled, especially in summer; tick-borne diseases are common in many dairy areas.
  • Dehorning or disbudding: done young, with pain relief as the vet advises, by trained staff.
  • Removal of extra teats: by trained staff or vet as the farm protocol says.

Handling safely and humanely

Move calves and heifers quietly, use crushes and head clamps correctly, and never hit, kick or twist tails. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 applies. Wear gloves when handling sick calves; some calf diseases, such as cryptosporidiosis and salmonellosis, can infect people. Wash hands thoroughly.

Records

Keep calf birth, colostrum, treatment, vaccination, weight and breeding records. Note product, dose and withdrawal period for every treatment.

Key points

  • Feed colostrum promptly and record it.
  • Mix milk accurately, feed at set times and clean equipment after every feed.
  • Check every calf daily and act early on illness.
  • Wean on starter intake and monitor growth against targets.
  • Follow the vet's vaccination, parasite and tick programmes and handle animals humanely.
